raw_text:
# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 60 million people worldwide and accounting for substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure [1]. Despite advances in guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), many patients remain symptomatic [2]. Importantly, CRT benefits are largely restricted to patients with prolonged QRS duration, leaving a large population with narrow QRS complexes without effective device-based options [3]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a device-based therapy designed to address this gap, particularly in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who have a narrow QRS [4].

## Mechanism of Action

CCM delivers non-excitatory electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period of the cardiac cycle [5]. Because these signals are timed to avoid initiating new action potentials, they do not provoke additional contractions but instead enhance the strength of the existing contraction [6]. The proposed mechanism involves modulation of intracellular calcium handling, with increased phosphorylation of phospholamban and improved sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling [7]. Experimental studies have demonstrated upregulation of key calcium-handling proteins and reversal of the fetal gene program associated with pathological remodeling [8]. These molecular changes translate into improved myocardial contractility without a proportional increase in myocardial oxygen consumption, distinguishing CCM from traditional positive inotropic agents [9].

## Clinical Evidence

Early proof-of-concept studies, including the FIX-HF-4 trial, demonstrated improvements in exercise tolerance and quality of life in patients receiving CCM [10]. The FIX-HF-5 trial evaluated CCM in patients with NYHA class III–IV HF and ejection fraction ≤35% [11]. While the primary endpoint of ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met in the overall cohort, a prespecified subgroup with ejection fraction between 25% and 45% showed significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption [12]. This finding informed the design of the subsequent FIX-HF-5C trial, which confirmed significant improvements in peak VO2, six-minute walk distance, and quality of life as measured by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [13]. A pooled analysis suggested potential reductions in HF hospitalizations among appropriately selected patients [14].

Long-term registries and observational cohorts have reported sustained symptomatic benefit and improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction over follow-up periods extending to several years [15]. The CCM-REG registry demonstrated reductions in HF hospitalizations and improvement in NYHA functional class in real-world populations [16]. Studies have also examined CCM in patients with HF and preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, an area of active investigation [17].

## Patient Selection

Current evidence supports CCM in patients with symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA class III) on optimal GDMT, with ejection fraction generally between 25% and 45%, and a narrow QRS duration (<130 ms) who are not candidates for CRT [18]. The Optimizer Smart system received regulatory approval in the United States in 2019 based on accumulated trial data [19]. Appropriate patient selection is essential, as benefits appear most consistent in those with intermediate reductions in ejection fraction [20].

## Safety and Device Considerations

CCM therapy delivered via implantable devices has demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with complication rates comparable to other implantable cardiac devices [21]. Importantly, CCM does not appear to increase ventricular arrhythmia burden, addressing early theoretical concerns about pro-arrhythmia from electrical stimulation during the refractory period [22]. Device-related complications include lead dislodgement and pocket infections, similar to pacemaker and defibrillator implantation [23]. Newer devices feature reduced charging requirements and improved battery longevity [24]. CCM can be combined with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators and CRT devices, though attention to device-device interactions is required [25].

## Quality of Life and Functional Outcomes

Consistent across trials is the improvement in patient-reported outcomes and functional capacity [26]. Meta-analyses synthesizing randomized data confirm improvements in peak VO2 and quality-of-life scores, with effect sizes that are clinically meaningful for symptomatic patients [27]. Some analyses suggest that CCM may favorably influence cardiac remodeling, with modest increases in ejection fraction over time [28].

## Future Directions and Conclusions

Ongoing trials aim to clarify the effects of CCM on hard endpoints such as mortality and HF hospitalization, and to define its role in HF with preserved ejection fraction [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses and longer-term comparative data with evolving pharmacotherapies, including SGLT2 inhibitors, will further refine its position in the treatment algorithm [30]. In summary, CCM represents a valuable therapeutic option for a subset of symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who remain limited despite optimal medical therapy, offering improvements in symptoms, functional capacity, and quality of life with an acceptable safety profile.
